# The Day My Van Almost Burned Down

On Wednesday, October 28th, around 2:15 in the afternoon, I was parked in a client's driveway in Bedford, drying Moose, a very large and very happy Bernese, on high. I smelled hot plastic and assumed it was the dryer motor. I've run that dryer for years and I know how it smells when it's working hard. This wasn't that.

Then I saw smoke coming out of the bench seat where my batteries are.

I shut off the battery switch, grabbed Moose by his harness, and got him out the side door while he was still damp. He was thrilled about it. Honestly, he was the only one of us having a good time. I used the fire extinguisher, though I'm not sure I needed to by the time I got to it. When I opened things up later, the positive lug on the battery cable was black, and the heat-shrink jacket had melted back about three centimetres.

Everyone is okay. Moose is fine, his mom is fine, and I'm fine physically. Mentally I'm a bit of a mess, and I'm writing this up now because a lot of you rely on this blog for van stuff, and because one of you, Tasha, is about to pay a deposit to the same person who built mine.

I'm not an electrician. I'm a mobile dog groomer in Halifax who ended up learning a lot more about 12-volt systems than I ever wanted to. What follows is what went wrong, what our electrician showed me, and what you can check on your own van this week. Please read the whole thing, and if you have any doubts about your own setup, get a professional to look at it.

## The setup

My van was built in spring 2025 by Coastline Van Fitouts. The build was done by Darren. It has a 3000W inverter, two 200Ah lithium batteries, and a 12V system. The van looked great. The bench was clean, the wiring looked tidy, and everything had that finished look that makes you feel like someone competent was in charge. I trusted it. In hindsight, that's the lesson I most want to share: **tidy is not the same as right.**

I run a dryer and sometimes the water heater off the inverter, which means the system works hard on every appointment, usually several times a day.

## What went wrong

After the fire, I got my van to Sackville Marine Electric and met with Priya, the electrician who went through the whole system with me. She was patient and clear, and she didn't make me feel stupid for not knowing this stuff. Here's what she found.

**The cable was too small.** The cable running from the battery to the inverter was 4 AWG. Priya's assessment was that for a 3000W inverter on a 12V system, it should have been 2/0. The difference between those two numbers matters a lot, and I'll explain why below.

**The lug was crimped badly.** The lug on the positive end was crimped with what looked like pliers or a hammer, not a proper hydraulic or ratcheting crimper. Heat-shrink was slid over the top, which made it look finished from the outside. You couldn't see the bad crimp unless you took the shrink off.

**The fuse was in the wrong place.** The 300A ANL fuse was mounted about 90cm from the battery. Priya said it should be within roughly 18cm of the battery terminal. The purpose of placing the fuse close to the battery is so that if something goes wrong along the cable, the cable is protected the whole way, not just the part near the inverter.

**There was no smoke alarm in the back.** The only smoke detector in the van was the one in the cab that came with the vehicle. Nothing was watching the battery bench.

When we compared my damage photos to thermal camera shots of Priya's own van running a similar load, the difference was wild. Hers barely gets warm. Mine had a hot spot at the lug that was hot enough to melt plastic. That contrast is the single most useful thing I got out of this whole ordeal.

## The numbers, in plain English

I'm going to try to explain this without making myself sound like an electrician, because I'm not one. But the numbers matter, so here they are.

Current in amps equals power in watts divided by voltage. At 12V, a 1800-2000W dryer pulls roughly 150 to 170 amps. Add the water heater running at the same time and the draw climbs toward 250 amps, and that's before you count the inverter's own losses. Running a 3000W inverter at full load on 12V means something close to 250 amps flowing through the cable.

Now think about what a cable does when it carries that much current. Every cable has resistance, and resistance turns current into heat. A thicker cable (lower AWG number, or in the case of 2/0, a much bigger size) has less resistance and produces less heat for the same current. The 4 AWG cable I had is much thinner than what the load needed. It was running hot the whole time, which is a slow problem, and then one day it became a fire problem.

The lug is where things get worse. A crimp that isn't tight enough creates a small area of high resistance where the cable meets the terminal. All that current squeezes through a tiny contact point, and that's where the heat concentrates. You can have a cable that's the right size and still get a hot spot if the connection is bad. That's exactly what happened at my lug.

The fuse placement is the third piece. A 300A fuse is designed to blow when current exceeds 300A. A 4 AWG cable is nowhere near rated to carry 300A safely. That means the fuse was never going to protect the cable from overheating. The cable could get into dangerous territory long before the fuse ever tripped. Priya's point was basically that the fuse and the cable need to be sized to match each other, and both need to be close to the battery.

The fourth piece is detection. Without a smoke alarm back there, I found out about the fire from the smell and the smoke, not from an alert.

I'm not going to pretend I understand every detail of the electrical code. I don't. But these four things, the cable size, the crimp, the fuse placement and rating, and the lack of detection, are what I'd want anyone else to look at first.

## What the repair looks like

The repair quote is $4,200. It covers rewiring the main runs, a new fuse block, and a Class T fuse, which is designed for high-current battery systems. Parts are on order and the job is at least three weeks. I've cancelled 31 appointments so far, which hurts in a way I can't fully describe. Every cancelled appointment is a dog who didn't get bathed and a client who has to find someone else, and a bunch of my regulars have been wonderfully understanding about it.

Insurance has said maybe, and an adjuster is supposed to look at the van. I'll update when I know more.

Darren hasn't answered three texts and an email. I'm stating that because it's a fact, and because people considering a build should know how it goes when something goes wrong. I'm not trying to trash anyone publicly. I'm saying what happened and letting people make their own decisions.

## What I should have checked

Here's the honest part. I didn't do anything wrong by trusting the person who built my van. I paid for a professional job and expected it to be done right. But I also never asked for the actual specs in writing. I didn't know what questions to ask.

Looking back, I should have asked:

- What gauge is the cable between the batteries and the inverter, and why that size for this inverter?
- What's the fuse rating, and where is it mounted?
- How were the lugs crimped, and with what tool?
- Is there a smoke or heat detector in the battery area?

If the answers are vague, or if the builder doesn't want to put them in writing, that's information.

## A checklist you can do on your own van, with the power off

Before you start, make sure the battery switch is off and the inverter is disconnected. Wear eye protection. Lithium batteries can deliver huge current if something shorts, so don't use metal tools across terminals, and don't work on the system with anything plugged in.

**1. Look at the main cable from the battery to the inverter.**
Find the gauge printed on the cable jacket. If it doesn't say, check the packaging or the paperwork from the build. Compare it to what your inverter manufacturer recommends for your wattage and voltage. If you can't tell, that's a question for a pro.

**2. Check the lugs.**
Look at every lug on the main battery cables, both positive and negative. Are they crimped with a proper crimping tool, or do they look flattened, hammered, or lumpy? Gently try to wiggle each cable at the lug. There should be no movement. Heat-shrink should be pushed back so you can see the crimp. If you can't see the crimp, that's a problem to fix.

**3. Look for discolouration.**
Check for black marks, browning, or melted jacket at every connection. Even a little discolouration around a lug is a warning sign.

**4. Check the fuse.**
Find the fuse on the positive cable. Measure roughly how far it is from the battery terminal. If it's much more than about 18cm, it's worth asking an electrician about moving it. Also confirm the fuse rating matches the cable's capacity, not just the inverter's wattage.

**5. Check the battery terminals.**
Make sure the nuts or bolts are tight, and that the terminals aren't corroded or loose. If you have the torque spec from the battery manufacturer, use it.

**6. Check the cable routing.**
Look at where the cables run. Are they touching anything hot? Are they rubbing on metal edges, or sitting against wood or foam where heat could build up? Are they secured so they can't move?

**7. Look for a smoke or heat detector near the batteries.**
Your cab detector is not enough for the battery area. A smoke alarm rated for vehicles, placed where it can actually sense the battery bench, is a cheap addition. You want to know about a problem before you can smell it.

**8. Use an infrared thermometer under load.**
This is the one I wish I'd had. I bought mine for $40 at Canadian Tire. With the inverter running a real load, like a hair dryer, a kettle, or a heater, check the temperature at the lugs, the fuse, and the battery terminals. Compare the readings to each other and to the cable jacket. A connection that's noticeably hotter than the rest is a hot spot. Don't wait until it smells.

**9. Note what you find and get it looked at.**
Take photos, write down cable gauges and fuse ratings, and bring them to an electrician. If anything looks off, don't keep running the system while you wait for an appointment.

## For Tasha, and anyone else about to buy a build

Tasha, I love you and I'm so glad you're thinking this through before the deposit. Before you pay anyone, ask for the following in writing:

- The cable gauge between the batteries and the inverter, and the reasoning for that size based on your inverter's wattage
- The fuse rating and the distance from the battery where it will be mounted
- How the lugs will be crimped, and with what tool
- Whether there's a smoke detector in the battery area
- The name of the electrician who will sign off on the electrical work, if there is one

If a builder can't or won't answer those questions clearly, you have your answer. A good builder will be happy to explain.

Also, please get a thermal or infrared check on any van you're buying second-hand. Ask the seller to run a load while you watch. If they won't, walk away.

## Where I'm at

I'm still in shock, if I'm being honest. Something I trusted almost took my van, and by extension my whole income, with a dog on the other end of it. I'm scared about rent, which is due on the 1st, and I'm trying to figure out how to keep my clients happy and my bills paid while I'm off the road.

I'm grateful for people in ways I didn't expect. Moose's mom made me a coffee and sat with me on her steps while I shook. My regulars have been patient. Priya was kind enough to show me exactly what went wrong, when she didn't have to.

I'm not an electrician, and this post isn't a substitute for one. If you have a van with a similar setup, please get it checked by a professional, even if it looks fine. Tidy isn't the same as right.

I'll post again when the van's back on the road. Until then, I'll be on my couch, keeping my fingers crossed, and maybe buying more infrared thermometers for the people I care about.
